title: Norfolk's street trees: the rules that protect them, and whether the City maintains them
summary: The City's own records show request-driven tree care with a documented backlog: in FY2021-FY2023 its budget reported fulfilling 5-9% of street-tree pruning requests, a draft City Auditor report says Forestry has been unable to adopt a proactive maintenance program, and the tree inventory has not been officially re-done since about 2000. They do not show that the City prefers cutting to maintaining: contracted work, an aging tree population, the pandemic, Dominion Energy and the Navy all play a part.

findings.claim: The City's FY2024 adopted budget reports that it fulfilled 5% of street-tree pruning requests in FY2021 (actual), 9% in FY2022 (actual) and 5% in FY2023 (projected), against 40% adopted for FY2024 and a 90% target. Requests received: 1,946, 1,367 and 1,436.

source.title: City of Norfolk FY2024 Adopted Budget, Department Budgets (Recreation, Parks and Open Space performance measures)

findings.quote: Percent of street tree pruning requests fulfilled

findings.claim: The researcher found the fulfillment measure absent from the FY2025 and FY2026 budget books, and the FY2027 book replaces pruning measures with trees planted. Not yet re-checked by a second reader.

source.title: City of Norfolk FY2027 Adopted Budget, Department Budgets

findings.claim: A City Auditor report on ground maintenance, marked DRAFT and dated April 2023, says Forestry has been unable to adopt a proactive tree maintenance program, and counts 1,408 tree work requests not completed at June 30, 2022. No final version was found.

source.title: Office of the City Auditor, Ground Maintenance audit report (DRAFT)

findings.quote: Forestry has been unable to adopt a pro-active tree maintenance program

findings.claim: The same draft audit says staff and equipment are not available for major tree work such as complete removal.

source.title: Office of the City Auditor, Ground Maintenance audit report (DRAFT)

findings.claim: In the FY2024 budget, a Forestry Supervisor ($119,572) that would let existing staff split into two crews was requested but not funded.

source.title: City of Norfolk FY2024 Adopted Budget, Department Budgets

findings.quote: The supervisor will allow the existing staff to be split into two crews

findings.claim: Norfolk's City Code (chapter 45) charges the City Forester with a forestry program that includes routine maintenance and with administering a street tree management plan; a 2019 report for the U.S. Forest Service and Virginia Department of Forestry found Norfolk had no urban forest management plan.

source.title: Green Infrastructure Center, Norfolk tree canopy and stormwater report (2019)

findings.quote: Norfolk does not currently have an UFMP

findings.claim: The same 2019 report says the City lacks the resources for a citywide tree assessment. The City's tree inventory describes itself as taken in the late 1990s/early 2000s with no official re-inventory since.

source.title: Green Infrastructure Center, Norfolk tree canopy and stormwater report (2019)

findings.quote: the city lacks the resource allocation to conduct a city-wide assessment

findings.claim: The City's urban forestry page says the main priority of its tree management is public safety, and rates work as Emergency, Urgent, Routine or Winter. It states no pruning cycle.

source.title: City of Norfolk, Urban Forestry

findings.quote: The main priority of the city's tree management is public safety

findings.claim: Not all tree work is in the work-order data: the FY2024 budget added $250,000 for a tree canopy maintenance contract used to remove decaying or diseased trees, and the draft audit counts $254,807 paid to an outside contractor for tree removal in FY2022. Pace figures from work orders alone overstate the gap.

source.title: City of Norfolk FY2024 Adopted Budget, Department Budgets

findings.quote: The contract is used to remove decaying or diseased trees

findings.claim: The FY2025 budget added $400,000 for tree maintenance to reduce a backlog it attributes to the pandemic.

source.title: City of Norfolk FY2025 Adopted Budget, Department Budgets

findings.quote: decrease the backlog of tree maintenance that built up during the pandemic

findings.claim: The draft audit attributes part of the backlog to Norfolk's aging tree population.

source.title: Office of the City Auditor, Ground Maintenance audit report (DRAFT)

findings.quote: aging tree population has contributed to

findings.claim: Not every removal is the City's: Dominion Energy clears neighborhood power lines on a four-year cycle, which can mean taking a whole tree.

source.title: Dominion Energy, tree trimming and power lines (Virginia)

findings.quote: Nearly all of our neighborhood power lines are cleared on a four year cycle

findings.claim: A 2014 national census of U.S. municipal forestry found a mean pruning cycle of 6.6 years among communities that use one, against a desired 4.8 years.

source.title: Hauer & Peterson, municipal tree care census, Arborist News (2016)

findings.claim: Norfolk's Tree Commission advises the City on trees; a researcher reported that City Code sec. 45-27 requires it to submit an annual report to the council. Not found on the Commission's page; not yet checked in the Code.

source.title: City of Norfolk, Tree Commission

findings.claim: Norfolk's Tree Ordinance makes it unlawful for anyone but the City's parks and forestry staff to plant, prune, remove, damage or disturb any tree on city-owned property, including the strip between curb and sidewalk, or to dig within a city tree's critical root zone, without a permit from the director (City Code sec. 45-13(b)).

source.title: Norfolk City Code chapter 45 (Trees), as abstracted April 2016 in Virginia Tech's Virginia Tree Ordinance Database; check the current code on Municode

findings.quote: it shall be unlawful for any person except an authorized employee of the bureau of parks and forestry to perform any of the following acts on city-owned property without first obtaining a permit from the director

findings.claim: Violating chapter 45 is a class 1 misdemeanor, each day counts as a new violation, and a judge may order the damage restored (City Code sec. 45-1).

source.title: Norfolk City Code chapter 45 (Trees), as abstracted April 2016 in Virginia Tech's Virginia Tree Ordinance Database; check the current code on Municode

findings.quote: Each day a violation continues shall be deemed a new violation

findings.claim: When trees are removed or damaged in violation of the ordinance, the director may require replacement, or accept a payment in lieu; that money, like permit fees, may be used only for urban forestry (City Code secs. 45-13(e), 45-11, 45-10).

source.title: Norfolk City Code chapter 45 (Trees), as abstracted April 2016 in Virginia Tech's Virginia Tree Ordinance Database; check the current code on Municode

findings.quote: shall be used solely for the purpose of enhancing urban forestry programs and operations

findings.claim: The ordinance's permit rule for trees on private land applies only in the Chesapeake Bay Preservation Area's resource protection and intensely developed areas (City Code sec. 45-13(c)); elsewhere, the abstract shows no permit needed to remove a private tree.

source.title: Norfolk City Code chapter 45 (Trees), as abstracted April 2016 in Virginia Tech's Virginia Tree Ordinance Database; check the current code on Municode

findings.quote: within the resource protection area or intensely developed areas in the Chesapeake Bay Preservation Area Overlay District without first obtaining a permit from the director

findings.claim: Residents may get a permit to prune city trees between curb and sidewalk themselves, after an arborist-led workshop, from the ground with hand tools (City Code sec. 45-13(a)).

source.title: Norfolk City Code chapter 45 (Trees), as abstracted April 2016 in Virginia Tech's Virginia Tree Ordinance Database; check the current code on Municode

findings.quote: Residents of Norfolk may apply for a permit to prune and trim city trees located between the curbs and sidewalks

findings.claim: The City Forester must direct a forestry program with preventative, corrective and routine maintenance, administer a street tree management plan, and propose the budget and staffing it needs (City Code sec. 45-4).

source.title: Norfolk City Code chapter 45 (Trees), as abstracted April 2016 in Virginia Tech's Virginia Tree Ordinance Database; check the current code on Municode

findings.quote: To direct a comprehensive municipal forestry program encompassing natural resource conservation, preventative, corrective and routine maintenance, and reforestation components

what_would_help.text: Fund the Forestry Supervisor the department requested for FY2024, so staff can work as two crews.
Restore the 'percent of pruning requests fulfilled' measure in the budget, so progress can be tracked.
Adopt the street tree management plan the City Code calls for, with a stated pruning cycle (communities using one average 6.6 years).
Fund a re-inventory with tree condition, so removals can be planned before trees fail.

records_to_request: All tree-care contracts and invoices from FY2020 to now, with trees pruned, removed and stump-ground per invoice.
A Forestry work-order export with the number of trees per order, request source, priority, and whether a City crew or a contractor did the work.
The open pruning-request backlog by priority and age, and the data behind the FY2021-FY2024 'requests fulfilled' measure.
Any street tree or urban forest management plan, pruning-cycle policy, and the final version of the 2023 Ground Maintenance audit.
Tree Commission annual reports and minutes since 2018.
pending: Canopy change 2014-2021 from the USGS/Chesapeake Conservancy 1-m land cover (researcher computed about -2.4%); not yet re-checked.
